questions.stem: Which three conditions does a seed need for germination?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
None of these is a taught germination condition.
Carbon dioxide is not needed before photosynthesis starts.
Soil and fertiliser are not required for germination itself.

questions.stem: Why does water help germination begin?

options.text: It supplies oxygen to the embryo
options.explanation: Oxygen enters as a gas, not inside water.

options.text: It swells the seed until the coat splits and the growth enzymes wake
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It feeds the seedling glucose directly
options.explanation: Water carries no glucose; the seed digests its own store.
The seed leaves are not dissolved.

questions.stem: In tube C, seeds sit under water covered by a layer of oil. Which condition has been removed?

options.explanation: Tube C is soaked — water is abundant there.
Oil does not destroy the seed's enzymes.

options.text: Oxygen, blocked by the water and oil layers
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Tube C stays at room temperature.

questions.stem: What role does the control tube play in this design?

options.explanation: Tube C tests oxygen removal.
Tube D tests warmth removal.
Tube A removes water; tube B removes nothing.

options.text: The control, with all three conditions present for comparison
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Which result would falsify the claim that all three conditions are needed?

options.text: Seeds germinating fully in tube A, C or D
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
That confirms the claim.
D germinating would falsify warmth's need, but B alone is expected — the falsifier is any removed-condition tube sprouting.
That suggests setup failure, not a condition refutation.

questions.stem: State what water does to the seed when germination starts.
questions.modelAnswer: Water swells the seed so the coat splits and the growth enzymes switch on.

questions.stem: Name the condition each test tube removes or keeps.
questions.modelAnswer: Tube A removes water, tube B is the control with all conditions, tube C blocks oxygen, and tube D removes warmth in the fridge.

questions.stem: Explain why warmth improves germination up to a point.
questions.modelAnswer: Warmth increases the activity of the enzymes that digest the seed's food store, so germination speeds up until higher temperatures start to denature them.

questions.stem: A student sets up a fifth tube with moist cotton wool on a warm windowsill in bright light. Predict and explain the outcome.
questions.modelAnswer: The seeds should germinate, because water, warmth and oxygen are all present, and light is not a required condition for germination.

questions.stem: How many cress seeds are placed in each test tube?

options.explanation: The method uses 10 seeds per tube.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Three is the day count window, not the seed count.
Four is the tube count, not the seed count.

questions.stem: Which tubes must stay moist through the 3 to 5 day observation window?

options.explanation: Tube A must stay dry for its test.
Tube D is moistened too and must not dry out.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
A is deliberately dry and C is flooded, not merely moist.

questions.stem: In the CORMS design, what does the letter O stand for in this investigation?

options.text: The oxygen level in each tube
options.explanation: Oxygen is the tested condition, not the letter O.
Observation is not what O encodes here.
Temperature sits under the S of CORMS.

options.text: The organism — cress seeds all taken from the same parent plant or species
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Why are the investigation repeats part of good design?

options.text: Repeating the investigation several times makes the results reliable
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Repeats do not change temperature.
The control stays in place.

options.text: Repeats change the organism each time
options.explanation: CORMS requires the same organism, not new ones.

questions.stem: Which CORMS element covers keeping tubes A, B and C at the same room temperature and using sterile water throughout?

options.explanation: R is running the trial again, not holding conditions steady.

options.text: S — controlling the sameness of everything except the tested factor
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
C is the condition being changed, not the ones held fixed.
M is counting germinated seeds after a set time.

questions.stem: State how long the seeds are left before comparing germination, and where tube D is kept.
questions.modelAnswer: The comparison happens after 3 to 5 days, and tube D is kept in a fridge.

questions.stem: State what is measured in each tube at the end of the practical.
questions.modelAnswer: The number of germinated seeds in each test tube is compared.

questions.stem: Explain why the seeds should all come from the same parent plant in this investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: Seeds from one parent plant keep the organism consistent, so germination differences reflect the tested condition rather than genetic variation between seeds.

questions.stem: A class finds three seeds sprouting in tube C after five days. Suggest one explanation and one improvement.
questions.modelAnswer: The oil layer may have left an air pocket giving some seeds oxygen, so the class should repeat the trial, pressing the layer down to seal fully and recounting with fresh seeds.
